title: How self-help gets reality wrong
subtitle: Reality and the self are perpetually incomplete
author: Christian Kumpost
introduction: There is a tension in religious and spiritual practices between focusing on self-improvement and neglecting the problems of the world. But Christian Kumpost argues that the root cause of this tension the belief that the self is what’s wrong with the world. We can resolve the tension between individualism and communitarianism, Kumpost suggests, by seeing the self and the world as not fundamentally wrong, but merely incomplete and ever evolving.
body:
Since the 1910 publication of a collection of various essays and articles written by G.K. Chesterton under the title What's Wrong With the World?, an anecdote has continually circulated—that in response to a newspaper’s query, “What's Wrong With the World?” Chesterton wrote in with a simple answer: “Dear Sirs, I am.” While it's clever in its simplicity, I believe its enduring quality lay not in it capturing the personality of Chesterton himself, but in it speaking to a deeper issue that has permeated the human experience—that everything wrong with the world is due to humanity itself, and the only solution to fixing the problems with the world (if that's even achievable), is to fix the problems within yourself. This is consistent whether a deeply rooted dogma or doctrine of a religious practice, or—at the risk of being crudely reductionistic—a kitschy tattoo or bumper sticker oft seen quoting Ghandi: “Be the change you wish to see in the world.”

SUGGESTED VIEWING The shadow of spirituality With Barry C. Smith, Sophie Grace Chappell, Michael Shermer, John Vervaeke

All too often, the problems of the world are at the same time both acknowledged as being the reality,  and dismissed as being impossible to fix. Broken people, broken world.  And so the anecdote about Chesterton's response to the question, “What's Wrong With the World?” has endured. It's speaks to a truth we feel: that things are not alright—something isn't right. Whether you look to the dominant Abrahamic religious traditions of the western world, or even to a lesser extent, Buddhism in the eastern world, both convey doctrines and dogmas correlating an inherent wrongness of the world with the wrongness of humanity itself.

The Abrahamic traditions (particularly Christianity) are predicated on the narrative that G-d originally created the world perfect and good and right, but due to mankind and original sin, not only has an inherent flaw passed down through humanity, but as a result, the world is now not as originally intended—it's fallen and broken as well. The doctrine of hamartia in Christianity, often translated as "sin nature," literally means "to miss the mark.” It's an archery term. Whether you know what the bullseye is or not, you are incapable of hitting the bullseye due to your sin nature. Because of this? Humanity itself cannot fix the world, only G-d can. And while some may call it a stretch, the four Noble Truths of Buddhism, too, speaks of dukkha, often interpreted as "suffering" or "unsatisfactoriness," as a fundamental aspect of existence, rooted in our desires and attachments. Both traditions suggest that the external chaos of the world is, in part, a reflection of internal turmoil.

When you are faced with a world of change that is overwhelming, it can make sense to choose to only focus on yourself.

I've seen a couple different versions of that story about Chesterton's response, but the closest I can find is that the quote itself comes from an article Chesterton had written for the Daily News, August 16, 1905. “In one sense, and that the eternal sense, the thing is plain. The answer to the question “What is Wrong?” is, or should be, “I am wrong.” Until a man can give that answer his idealism is only a hobby.” I'd posit that the meaning of “idealism as a hobby” is that it does nothing and benefits no one outside of yourself.

And when you are faced with a world of change that is overwhelming, it can make sense to choose to only focus on yourself. Much like the chorus of the song by Ten Years After states: “I'd love to change the world, but I don't know what to do. So I'll leave it up to you.” This we see as the predominant reaction taken by most major religions. Close your eyes and look within (like those statues of Buddha), or sequester and isolate yourselves from the broken sinful world, waiting for G-d to return, like the Christians.

What happens when our focus on inner contemplation leads us away from the pressing issues of the world around us? Or contrastingly, what happens when our focus on the pressing issues of the world around us lead us to ignore the self—quite possibly the very root of those pressing world issues?

SUGGESTED VIEWING Rethinking Science and Spirituality With Rupert Sheldrake

Do you hate the state of yourself and feel a desire for change? Any bookshop or online resource will lead you to swathes of options available. And if self-help books don't do the trick, you can always turn to religion. All the same thing, really, self-improvement through the promise of reaching fulfillment—whether through your own efforts, or through something more divine and supernatural.
And when those promised solutions don't work, then what? It's because you're not doing it right. You're wrong. Just work harder at it. Focus more on self. Read a different self-help book. Try a different program. Isolate more into your religious practice.

Or maybe the problem with you isn't you. Maybe it's the world around you. And you need to isolate yourself from that wrongness in order to be right.

Or maybe you need to change it. Change the world. Make it right in order for you to be right. Just go online and open up any social media platform to not only find swathes of opinions on what is wrong with the world, or who exactly the problem is, but what we need to do collectively to fix it. As an American citizen, this has been the unavoidable focal point of politics and media for the past 10 years at least. It's difficult to find something that doesn't have any comments on its correlation to the greater state of what's wrong with the world.

The real issue at hand is a matter of *focus—*which is to say, the real issue at hand is a question of clarity—depending on what you choose to focus on. You see, depending on your focal point, whatever you're not focusing on becomes blurred and distorted. As a single parent, I'm constantly questioning what I'm doing wrong, how I can be better, and how I can juggle the balance between care for my two kids, and my own self-care. There's a tension of values between the two, especially when I'm already feeling neglected and have to interrupt my self-care routine in order to mitigate the conflict and issues that arise between the two of them. I'm striving to raise healthy, independent, loving and aware human beings that aren't assholes, but I also don't want it to come at the cost of my own neglect. How do I balance loving and caring and concerning myself with taking care of my kids, with loving and caring and concerning myself with myself? I don't think the two are mutually exclusive, but when I'm at the end of my rope and completely overwhelmed, focusing on one comes entirely at the expense of ignoring the other.

Whatever is chosen to focus on (and perhaps get too caught up focusing solely on), the root of the matter lay in one simple feeling: Something is not right. Something is off. Things are not how they should be. And this is the impetus and motivation for change—whether change of self or change of the world: to right the wrong. To make your wrong self right. To make the wrong world, right.

To frame the human condition as one of perpetual incompletion, rather than inherent flaw, shifts the narrative from one of despair to one of hopeful striving.

In cinematography, a split diopter is a partial lens that attaches to a standard camera lens and features at least two different focal planes. This lens attachment has the effect of greatly expanding the depth of field so that the immediate foreground and the distant background can both be in sharp focus. This means that there is no distortion, all things are clear.

Perhaps it isn't an issue of impossible contradictions, perhaps we simply need to find the split diopter to apply. The original question of “What's wrong with the world?” (And its answer of “I am”) presupposes not only that there is something wrong with the world, but that there is something wrong with myself. Furthermore, the reason for the wrongness of the world is the wrongness of self. Thus, the solution to fixing the wrong world, is to fix the wrong self.

But what if this assumption—that both the world and our selves are inherently flawed—misses a crucial point? What if the issue is not one of fundamental brokenness or wrongness, but of incompleteness? To frame the human condition as one of perpetual incompletion, rather than inherent flaw, shifts the narrative from one of despair to one of hopeful striving. What if the problem lay in both the original question and its answer? And the solution is in asking a different question.

This idea resonates deeply with the work of Sigmund Freud, Jacques Lacan, and Simone Weil. Freud's concept of the pleasure principle is often misunderstood as merely an obsession with sex, but it's really about seeking pleasure and avoiding pain. However, he observed that people often engage in self-destructive behaviors, leading him to propose the death drive—a hidden force driving us toward destruction and nothingness. Lacan expanded on this, suggesting that our sense of self, formed in the "mirror stage," introduces a feeling of lack that stays with us throughout life. This lack drives our desires, which we believe will complete us, but the void remains. Lacan's "objet petit a" represents those unattainable desires, standing in for our deeper sense of incompleteness.

But when I am allowed to see and believe that I'm not wrong, just incomplete, then the world is also not wrong, it's just incomplete.

Simone Weil deepens this understanding by emphasizing that our suffering is rooted not just in what we lack, but in the very nature of our desires. Weil argues that we are, by our very nature, creatures of lack—constantly yearning for something beyond ourselves. She suggests that this constant yearning is what drives us, but it is also what causes us to suffer. In my teaching, I explore this notion of ateleology—the idea that we are inherently incomplete, and that this incompletion is not a flaw, but an ontological reality.

The human condition is characterized by this ontological void. We are creatures of lack, driven by the death drive to fill that void. However, the real issue isn't our incompleteness, but the presupposition because of that incompletion, we're broken and thus, wrong. If we accept that we are inherently incomplete, we realize that being incomplete doesn't mean being broken or wrong.

I can't fix a broken world when I'm too preoccupied with fixing a broken self. I can't right the wrongs of the world when I am constantly under a belief system that tells me I am what's wrong with the world. But when I am allowed to see and believe that I'm not wrong, just incomplete, then the world is also not wrong, it's just incomplete. The world’s problems and our personal struggles may not stem from inherent flaws, but from the ongoing process of becoming that defines existence. To view both as incomplete rather than broken is to embrace a philosophy of hope and continuous improvement. We are not here to fix a broken world or mend a broken self, but to participate in the ongoing creation of both, with the understanding that this process is, by nature, cyclically never-ending.

If you want to bridge the alleged opposition between self-improvement on the one hand, and communitarianism on the other, ask a different question:

What's right with the world? I am.

But I could always be better, and so could the world.
